concept.name: Diversification
concept.definition: A risk-management strategy of spreading money across different investments - both between and within asset categories - so that losses in one holding may be offset by gains or stability in others, reducing portfolio-level volatility.
concept.intuition: Don't put all your eggs in one basket: if one investment loses money, the hope is that the others make up for it.
concept.mechanics: Because portfolio variance contains covariance terms, combining assets whose returns are imperfectly correlated yields a portfolio volatility below the weighted average of individual volatilities; this removes much asset-specific (idiosyncratic) risk but cannot remove market-wide (systematic) risk.
concept.failure_modes: Diversification works least when it is most needed: correlations across markets rise in bear markets and crises, so apparently diversified portfolios can fall together. It reduces risk but does not eliminate the risk of loss.
concept.misconceptions: Holding several investments is not the same as being diversified - a handful of stocks in one sector, or several funds holding the same stocks, leaves concentrated exposure intact.
concept.example: A total stock market index fund holding thousands of companies diversifies away most single-company risk, while adding a bond fund diversifies across asset categories.

citations.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Beginners' Guide to Asset Allocation, Diversification, and Rebalancing
